analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: How Will Higher Rates Affect the US Economy?
key_insights: GS baseline assumes one more Fed hike in December, then three cuts starting in 2027H2 (September 2027). 10-year Treasury yields ease from 5.3% today to 4.4% by end-2027. GS also gauges the risks if current rates persist.

Rates have risen sharply since the start of the Iran War (February 27, 2026). The GS US financial conditions index moved sideways for a few months as higher equity prices, tighter credit spreads and a weaker dollar offset higher long rates, but it is now tightening.

Higher rates weigh most on residential investment per dollar of GDP, but consumer spending (about 65% of GDP) and capex (about 15%) contribute meaningfully to the overall drag because they are larger shares than residential investment (about 5%).

Residential investment: higher rates are expected to subtract about 2pp from annualized growth at the 2026Q4 peak and about 1pp on average in 2027. The drag would be roughly twice as large if rates stayed at current levels.

Mortgage rates are up more than 1pp since February. Over 90% of borrowers hold mortgages priced below the current market rate, which deepens lock-in and discourages moving. Survey-based purchase intentions have declined since early summer.

Consumer spending: higher rates are estimated to slow growth by about 0.2pp in 2027 in the baseline. A durables demand drag is partly offset by higher net interest income, since households are net lenders in aggregate. The drag would rise substantially if current rates persisted.

A 50bp rise in the fed funds rate has historically lowered consumer spending by slightly less than 0.5%, concentrated in durable goods, especially recreation goods and motor vehicles. GS expects the current impact to be smaller because of strong household balance sheets and limited negative wealth effects.

Capex: higher refinancing costs are expected to cut capex growth by about 0.3pp in 2027 and in subsequent years. The impact would be more than double if rates stayed higher. Small businesses are more exposed because about half their debt is variable-rate.

About 15% of corporate bonds mature within two years, roughly in line with recent years and below the historical average. Average corporate debt maturity has roughly doubled over three decades, which slows passthrough from fed funds hikes to corporate borrowing costs.

AI capex: hyperscaler capex, over two-thirds of AI-related US investment, has been largely insensitive to higher rates and input costs. GS reads this as high hurdle rates and little near-term pullback. GS portfolio strategists expect healthy AI capex in 2027, and credit strategists raised hyperscaler debt issuance forecasts.

Total GDP effect: higher rates subtract about 0.2pp from 2027 Q4/Q4 GDP growth in the baseline, leaving growth close to GS's 2.3% potential estimate. If current rates persist, the drag rises to slightly over 0.5pp. The financial conditions framework currently implies only a 0.1pp hit to 2026Q4/Q4 GDP growth.

Equity risk: rate-sensitive segments (unprofitable tech, utilities, REITs, homebuilders) have pulled back sharply from highs, and broad indices have been roughly flat since August. GS strategists expect equities to edge higher through end-2026 and rise about 10% in 2027, but stable rates could limit upside. Flat equities through 2027 would lower consumer spending growth by just under 0.5pp.

Fiscal risk: r-g (average interest rate on government debt minus nominal GDP growth) stays negative in the baseline but would turn positive by 2030 if current market rates persisted. Debt-to-GDP would reach 132% by 2035, 10pp above the baseline, raising the odds that deficit reduction becomes necessary sooner.

risk_factors: If current rates persist, the GDP growth drag rises to slightly over 0.5pp in 2027, versus about 0.2pp in the baseline.
Equities could stall if rates stay high. Flat equities through 2027 would lower consumer spending growth by just under 0.5pp through a smaller wealth effect.
Fiscal sustainability: r-g would turn positive by 2030 if current market rates persisted, and debt-to-GDP would reach 132% by 2035, 10pp above baseline.
Small businesses are more exposed to higher rates because about half their debt is variable-rate and reprices quickly.
Residential investment: the drag would be roughly twice as large if rates stayed at current levels, and mortgage lock-in suppresses housing turnover.
AI capex could become more rate-exposed over time because heavy AI spending has eroded free cash flow and pushed firms toward debt and equity issuance.
vol_and_positioning: Rate-sensitive equity segments (unprofitable tech, utilities, REITs, homebuilders) have pulled back sharply from their highs, while broad indices have been roughly flat since August.
geopolitical: Rates have risen sharply since the start of the Iran War, with February 27, 2026 used as the pre-war baseline for the yield curve and mortgage rate comparisons.

tension_points.bull_case: In the baseline, long rates fall from 5.3% to 4.4% by end-2027, the drag on 2027 GDP is only about 0.2pp, and growth stays near the 2.3% potential estimate. Equities rise about 10% in 2027 and hyperscaler capex has been insensitive to rates.
tension_points.bear_case: If current rates persist, the GDP drag rises to slightly over 0.5pp. Equities could stall, which would cut consumer spending growth by just under 0.5pp. The debt-to-GDP ratio would reach 132% by 2035.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Long-term rates failing to ease from the current 5.3% 10-year yield toward the 4.4% end-2027 forecast, with equities roughly flat through 2027.
